London, 9<sup>th</sup> April 2009 



# Norilsk Nickel Daily News Digest 

**The White House task force** charged with retooling the U.S. auto industry is meeting with General Motors officials to accelerate its restructuring process, an administration official said Wednesday. _Source:  Automotive News_ 

**Cash-strapped auto suppliers** may be able to tap the full $5 billion in U.S. aid designated for their relief, even if Ford doesn’t take its allocation of the funds.   The spokeswoman’s statement clarifies a point of confusion as to whether the unclaimed Ford allocation would be made available to GM and Chrysler. The actual amount available through GM and Chrysler will depend on how much each automaker seeks to tap. The companies have to pay a 5% fee to the U.S. Treasury for the funds. General Motors will have to pay $100 million into the supplier bailout program, or 5% of the $2 billion that GM currently plans to tap for its suppliers. For Chrysler’s $1.5 billion share of the program, the amount would be $75 million.  Ford said that it had enough cash for suppliers, so it did not need to participate in the programme.  Suppliers can either pay a 3 % fee to get paid quicker than the normal 45 days for parts already delivered, or use the funds to guarantee their receivables as collateral for loans. _Source:  Automotive News_ 

**U.S. auto industry sales** are expected to be equal to or slightly better in the second quarter than in Q1 09, Toyota’s U.S. President Jim Lentz said.  Lentz said U.S. auto industry sales in April so far have been similar to March.  Automakers reported sales approaching a 9.9 million vehicle annualized rate in March, a bump up from rates seen in the first two months of the year, but still far below the 15.1 million rate a year earlier.  The sales rate during the first quarter was 9.5 million units.  Auto industry sales could rise by at least 1 million vehicles in 2010, though demand could be boosted further in the near term if the United States adopts fleet modernization incentives, Lentz said.  Toyota has no plans at present to match the incentive programs of Hyundai, GM and Ford, which cover car payments in case of job loss. _Source:  Automotive News_ 

**China’s passenger car sales** rose 10% in March from a year earlier after tax cuts and government subsidies boosted demand, narrowing the gap with the U.S. as the world’s largest car market.  Sales of cars, minivans and multi-purpose vehicles rose to a record 772,400 in the month, according to China Association of Automobile Manufacturers. Sales of cars and light trucks in the U.S. plunged 37% last month to 857,399 vehicles.  Demand for minivans surged 40% last month as the government began giving out 5 billion yuan ($731 million) in subsidies to help rural residents buy vans and light trucks. Including trucks and buses, vehicle sales rose 5% to 1.11 million units in March, a monthly record.   GM said its China sales hit a record of 137,004 units last month, up 25% fro

m 2007. GM aims to double annual China sales to more than 2 million vehicles over the next five years. The company will introduce more than 30 new and upgraded models in the country in the next five years.   Daimler boosted Mercedes sales in China 30% in the first quarter from a year earlier. Total vehicle sales in China rose 3.88 % to 2.68 million units in the first quarter.  Commercial-vehicle sales fell 5.3% last month to 337,400 while they fell 6.1% to 683,100 in the first quarter. Minivan sales last month were 165,600 units. The country’s total vehicle exports fell 62 % in Q109 to 61,000 units because of global financial crisis.  Beijing Hyundai Motor Co said its total stockpile on April 7 from both factories and dealers was 33,500 units, equivalent 80% of monthly sales. 

_Source:  Bloomberg_ 

**Yageo and Holy Stone** have reported sequential revenue increases of 23% and 14%, respectively, for March, thanks to a warming up of demand.  Industry sources indicated that suppliers are considering raising quotes for multi-layer ceramic-chip capacitors (MLCCs) because of tight supply. _Source:  Digtimes_
